extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political economy (general educated public, economists)
extracted.subtask_description: Close-reading and extraction of evaluative principles from a classical-political-economy discussion about the relationships among wages, population growth, and national prosperity (Adam Smith–style economic analysis).

rubrics_metrics.name: The most decisive mark of the prosperity of any country is the increase of the number of its inhabitants.
rubrics_metrics.description: The most decisive mark of the prosperity of any country is the increase of the number of its inhabitants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explained with empirical comparisons: in Great Britain and most of Europe populations double very slowly (e.g., five hundred years), while in British North America they double in twenty or twenty-five years. Population increase is attributed not principally to immigration but to higher fertility and the economic value of children where labour is well rewarded; examples include many descendants, young marriage ages, and the labour-value of children's contributions (e.g., each child's labour before leaving home computed as 'a hundred pounds clear gain').

rubrics_metrics.name: The liberal reward of labour is the necessary effect and natural symptom of increasing national wealth.
rubrics_metrics.description: The liberal reward of labour, therefore, as it is the necessary effect, so it is the natural symptom of increasing national wealth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: higher wages both reflect and cause increased population and industry. Higher pay encourages marriage and reproduction and increases industry and productivity. To lament higher wages is to lament the signs of public prosperity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scanty maintenance of the labouring poor is the symptom of stagnation; starvation is the symptom of decline.
rubrics_metrics.description: The scanty maintenance of the labouring poor, on the other hand, is the natural symptom that things are at a stand, and their starving condition, that they are going fast backwards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by examples (China, Bengal, English settlements in the East Indies): decaying 'funds destined for the maintenance of labour' produce famine, mortality, and shrinking population; large mortality and mass destitution indicate that the economic resources available to maintain labour are falling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seasonal wage differences indicate wages are above mere subsistence regulation.
rubrics_metrics.description: First, in almost every part of Great Britain there is a distinction, even in the lowest species of labour, between summer and winter wages. Summer wages are always highest. But, on account of the extraordinary expense of fuel, the maintenance of a family is most expensive in winter. Wages, therefore, being highest when this expense is lowest, it seems evident that they are not regulated by what is necessary for this expense, but by the quantity and supposed value of the work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If wages were set at mere subsistence, they would be proportional to daily necessities (e.g., higher in winter when fuel costs rise). The observed seasonal premium implies wages respond to demand/quantity/value of work rather than immediate subsistence needs (contrast with slave-maintenance proportionality).

rubrics_metrics.name: If wages do not fluctuate with prices of provisions, they are not fixed by subsistence needs.
rubrics_metrics.description: Secondly, the wages of labour do not, in Great Britain, fluctuate with the price of provisions. These vary everywhere from year to year, frequently from month to month. But in many places, the money price of labour remains uniformly the same, sometimes for half a century together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequence: when wages remain stable while provisions become dearer or cheaper, labourers' real standard of living changes with provisions price — indicating wages are not set at a subsistence floor but by other factors (e.g., demand for labour). The text uses this as evidence wages are above the minimum necessary for family maintenance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wages vary more from place to place than prices of provisions do.
rubrics_metrics.description: Thirdly, as the price of provisions varies more from year to year than the wages of labour, so, on the other hand, the wages of labour vary more from place to place than the price of provisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: London and neighbourhood wages markedly higher than nearby rural areas; Edinburgh vs surrounding low-country Scotland. This geographic wage dispersion shows local labour demand and conditions drive wages more than uniform subsistence costs, and that human mobility does not quickly equalize wages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variations in the price of labour can be opposite to variations in the price of provisions.
rubrics_metrics.description: Fourthly, the variations in the price of labour not only do not correspond, either in place or time, with those in the price of provisions, but they are frequently quite opposite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by grain and labour: grain may be dearer in Scotland than in England, yet labour is cheaper in Scotland than in England. Conclusion: wages are largely determined by demand for labour, quality, and local industry rather than by local cost of subsistence.

rubrics_metrics.name: The price of labour cannot be ascertained very accurately and law cannot properly regulate it.
rubrics_metrics.description: The price of labour, it must be observed, cannot be ascertained very accurately anywhere, different prices being often paid at the same place and for the same sort of labour, not only according to the different abilities of the workman, but according to the easiness or hardness of the masters. Where wages are not regulated by law, all that we can pretend to determine is, what are the most usual; and experience seems to shew that law can never regulate them properly, though it has often pretended to do so.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical guidance: wage assessment should rely on observed customary wages and local practice; legislative attempts to fix wages are ineffective because of heterogeneity of individual ability and employer conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Real recompense (purchasing power) of labour matters more than nominal money wage.
rubrics_metrics.description: The real recompence of labour, the real quantity of the necessaries and conveniencies of life which it can procure to the labourer, has, during the course of the present century, increased perhaps in a still greater proportion than its money price.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence: many food items and coarse manufactures became cheaper (potatoes, turnips, carrots, coarse linen and woollens), improving workers' standards of living even if nominal wages changed less. Evaluation of labourers' condition should therefore consider purchasing power and availability of goods, not only nominal wages.

rubrics_metrics.name: What improves the circumstances of the greater part of the people is an advantage to society.
rubrics_metrics.description: Servants, labourers, and workmen of different kinds, make up the far greater part of every great political society. But what improves the circumstances of the greater part, can never be regarded as any inconveniency to the whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Normative guidance: social policy and appraisals of economic change should treat rising material welfare of the majority as a public good; equity and practical justice demand labourers receive a fair share of the produce of their labour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Population multiplies in proportion to the means of subsistence.
rubrics_metrics.description: Every species of animals naturally multiplies in proportion to the means of their subsistence, and no species can ever multiply beyond it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied to humans: in civilized societies limits to population growth operate mainly through scarcity among the lower ranks, expressed in high child mortality and exposure of infants; thus demography is constrained by available resources for rearing children.

rubrics_metrics.name: The demand for labour regulates the production of men (population growth).
rubrics_metrics.description: The demand for men, like that for any other commodity, necessarily regulates the production of men, quickens it when it goes on too slowly, and stops it when it advances too fast.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mechanism: rising demand for labour raises wages and encourages marriage and higher birth rates among labouring classes to match labour demand; if reward too low, population falls until wage rises; if reward too high, over-multiplication reduces wages. Market equilibrating force governs population to meet labour demand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Work done by freemen is cheaper in the end than that performed by slaves.
rubrics_metrics.description: The work done by freemen comes cheaper in the end than that performed by slaves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: differences in management (slave-replacement funds mismanaged vs frugal self-management by freemen) mean freemen maintain themselves more effectively and their labour yields lower long-run costs. Illustrated with examples from Boston, New-York, and Philadelphia.

rubrics_metrics.name: Progressive societies give the happiest condition to the labouring poor; stationary/declining states are worse.
rubrics_metrics.description: It deserves to be remarked, perhaps, that it is in the progressive state, while the society is advancing to the further acquisition, rather than when it has acquired its full complement of riches, that the condition of the labouring poor, of the great body of the people, seems to be the happiest and the most comfortable. ... The progressive state is, in reality, the cheerful and the hearty state to all the different orders of the society; the stationary is dull; the declining melancholy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use as evaluative criterion for national condition: rising economic activity and growth improve the material and psychological well-being of most classes, while stagnation or decline produces poverty and misery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Higher wages generally encourage industry, but excessive piece-work can harm health and long-term output.
rubrics_metrics.description: The wages of labour are the encouragement of industry... Where wages are high, accordingly, we shall always find the workmen more active, diligent, and expeditious... when they are liberally paid by the piece, are very apt to overwork themselves, and to ruin their health and constitution in a few years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balanced judgement: although better pay motivates productivity and skill, piece-rate systems may produce short-term overwork and occupational infirmities (examples: carpenters lasting only eight years, soldiers' excessive earnings requiring caps on daily pay). Employers and policy should consider moderation to preserve long-run labour capacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cheap vs dear years affect employment composition and bargaining power between masters and servants.
rubrics_metrics.description: In cheap years servants frequently leave their masters, and trust their subsistence to what they can make by their own industry... Farmers, upon such occasions, expect more profit from their corn by maintaining a few more labouring servants... In years of scarcity, the difficulty and uncertainty of subsistence make all such people eager to return to service... the wages of both servants and journeymen frequently sink in dear years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation of cyclical effects: cheap seasons raise the fund for maintaining servants and can increase demand for labour and independent workmen, while dear seasons reduce funds, increase labour supply for hire, and strengthen masters' bargaining position. Use manufactured-output records and employment patterns to test these effects.
